issues.legal_issue: An authorized officer may extend the time for an auction purchaser to pay the balance sale price within the statutory maximum period, but the purchaser has no right to an extension, and refusal is reviewable where exceptional circumstances show the decision-making process was arbitrary or unreasonable.

Forfeiture of an auction purchaser’s deposit under Rule 9(5) is a statutory penalty that may be challenged, but courts should interfere only in exceptional cases and should not base intervention solely on a later resale at the same or a higher price or the absence of financial loss.
Rule 9(5) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules operates alongside the general law of contract, and in case of conflict or inconsistency the SARFAESI Act and its rules prevail.
Retention of a deposit forfeited under Rule 9(5) does not constitute unjust enrichment where the forfeiture is authorized by statute and follows the purchaser’s default.

A writ court should not set aside a statutory forfeiture absent a clear case of arbitrariness, mala fides, bias, or irrationality, or intervene merely to protect private interests at the expense of public interests.
